title: The Importance of Denied Party Screening and the BIS Affiliate Rule
summary: Denied Party Screening is a critical component of compliance. Understand the potential changes to the BIS Affiliate Rule before they go into effect.
body_markdown:
Global trade compliance has always been a moving target, but one thing remains constant: the importance of knowing exactly who you're doing business with. As sanctions, export controls, and restricted party requirements continue to evolve, Denied Party Screening (DPS) is no longer just a compliance exercise. It is a critical part of protecting revenue, safeguarding reputation, and ensuring business continuity.


Recent regulatory changes have placed even greater attention on ownership structures and affiliated entities. The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) introduced an Affiliates Rule that would extend export control restrictions to entities that are 50% or more owned, directly or indirectly, by organizations appearing on the Entity List, Military End User (MEU) List, or certain sanctioned party lists. The suspension of the BIS Affiliate Rule (also referred to as the BIS 50% rule) is currently set to expire on November 9, although another pause or postponement remains possible. Regardless of any decision made on that date, importers should begin taking proactive steps now to ensure they are prepared.


**The "What If" Scenario: What if BIS Affiliates Rule goes into effect?**


Organizations that rely solely on traditional denied party screening may find themselves exposed, as many screening tools identify only explicitly listed entities. Under a BIS affiliate ownership framework, the compliance responsibility shifts beyond screening of named parties to include entities connected through ownership and control relationships.


Risk mitigation in this scenario is not just about screening names; it is understanding corporate relationships and hidden ownership exposure. In practice, this means businesses could unknowingly transact with a company that appears "clean" on the surface but is restricted due to its ownership structure. The result of missing sanctioned parties could include shipment delays, export licensing issues, compliance investigations, financial penalties, and reputational damage.


**Why Screening Matters Regardless**


In a world where compliance requirements can change overnight, readiness and adaptability are competitive advantages.


Whether the BIS pause is extended or allowed to expire, the need for stronger due diligence remains. Global networks and entities are complex and, unfortunately, some will look for ways to circumvent regulations. Importers need to be meticulous in research and record keeping to stay compliant. As stricter regulations arise, importers need to adapt their processes and tools to meet requirements and avoid penalties.


**What’s Next?**


As screening requirements continue to evolve, organizations will benefit from tools that support consistent due diligence, improve data visibility, and help manage compliance activities more efficiently.


Expeditors’ compliance software **[Tradeflow](https://www.tradeflow.com/)** helps organizations stay ahead by centralizing trade partner data, automating screening processes, and providing a system of record for compliance activities. Tradeflow users can gain access to Kharon's Sanctions 50-Plus and BIS 50-Plus datasets, helping identify entities owned or controlled by sanctioned or export-restricted parties that may not appear on traditional denied party lists. This additional visibility into hidden ownership risks can help importers enhance screening efforts and better assess potential compliance exposure.
